items.title: The Five Dynasties (1206–1526) & Ghurid Foundation
items.body:
## From the Ghurid conquest to the Sultanate

- The Ghurid ruler **Muhammad Ghuri** lost the **First Battle of Tarain (1191)** to **Prithviraj Chauhan** but won the decisive **Second Battle of Tarain (1192)**; the **Battle of Chandawar (1194)** crushed **Jaichandra** of Kannauj.
- **Bakhtiyar Khalji** overran Bihar and Bengal (defeating **Lakshman Sena**) and destroyed its Buddhist monasteries. On Ghuri's death in **1206**, his slave-governor **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** declared independence — founding the Delhi Sultanate.

## The five dynasties

| Dynasty | Period | Founder |
|---|---|---|
| Slave / Mamluk | 1206–1290 | Qutb-ud-din Aibak |
| Khalji | 1290–1320 | Jalaluddin Khalji |
| Tughlaq | 1320–1414 | Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq |
| Sayyid | 1414–1451 | Khizr Khan |
| Lodi | 1451–1526 | Bahlol Lodi |

- The Sultanate ended when **Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**.
keyPoints: First Battle of Tarain (1191) = Prithviraj's win; Second Battle of Tarain (1192) = Muhammad Ghuri's decisive victory.
Battle of Chandawar (1194) defeated Jaichandra (Gahadavala) of Kannauj; Tarain + Chandawar founded Turkish rule in North India.
Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 when Qutb-ud-din Aibak declared independence after Ghuri's death.
Five dynasties in order: Slave (1206) → Khalji (1290) → Tughlaq (1320) → Sayyid (1414) → Lodi (1451).
The Sultanate ended at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur defeating Ibrahim Lodi.
items.mnemonic: Dynasty order 'Slave Kings Take Some Land' = Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.

items.title: Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty — Aibak to Balban
items.body:
## Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210)

- First Sultan of Delhi; called **Lakh Baksh** ('giver of lakhs'); began the **Qutub Minar** and built the **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque (Delhi) and **Adhai-din-ka-Jhonpra** (Ajmer). Court based at **Lahore**; died in a polo (chaugan) fall.

## Iltutmish (1211–1236) — the real consolidator

- Shifted the capital from **Lahore to Delhi**; issued the first pure Arabic **silver tanka** and copper **jital**; organised the **iqta** system (revenue assignments) and the **Turkan-i-Chihalgani** (Council of Forty). Completed the Qutub Minar; nominated **Razia** as successor.

## Razia Sultana (1236–1240)

- **First and only woman** to rule Delhi; efficient, but opposed by the Turkish nobles; married **Altunia** to recover power and was defeated and killed.

## Balban (1266–1287)

- Enforced a **'blood and iron'** policy; introduced **sijda** (prostration) and **paibos** (kissing the feet); exalted the king as **Zill-i-Ilahi** (Shadow of God); broke the **Chihalgani** and defeated the Bengal rebel **Tughril Beg**; patronised **Amir Khusrau**.
keyPoints: Qutb-ud-din Aibak = first Sultan, 'Lakh Baksh', began Qutub Minar; capital at Lahore.
Iltutmish shifted capital to Delhi, issued the silver tanka, organised the iqta system and the Chihalgani (Council of Forty).
Razia Sultana (1236–1240) was the first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.
Balban's 'blood and iron' policy, sijda and paibos, and the Zill-i-Ilahi ideal exalted royal authority.
Balban broke the power of the Chihalgani and crushed the Bengal rebel Tughril Beg.

items.title: Khalji Dynasty & Alauddin's Reforms
items.body:
## Founding

- **Jalaluddin Khalji** founded the dynasty in **1290**, ruling mildly from **Kilokhri**; he was assassinated in **1296** by his nephew and son-in-law **Alauddin Khalji** after the Devagiri raid — the 'Khalji revolution'.

## Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) — conquests

- **North:** Gujarat (1299 raid, 1304 annexed), **Ranthambore (1301)**, **Chittor (1303)**, **Malwa (1305)**, Siwana (1308), Jalore (1311); repelled repeated **Mongol** invasions.
- **Deccan (under Malik Kafur):** **Devagiri** (Yadava), **Warangal** (Kakatiya — gifted the Kohinoor), **Dwarasamudra** (Hoysala), **Madurai** (Pandya) — tribute-raids that enriched Delhi.

## Reforms

- **Market/price control:** fixed low prices to fund a cheap army; three markets — grain **mandi**, cloth **Sarai Adl**, and horses/slaves/cattle — under the **Shahna-i-Mandi**; the **Diwan-i-Riyasat** registered every merchant; spies (**Barid, munhiyans**) reported daily.
- **Military:** first to keep a **large standing army paid in cash**, with the **Dagh** (horse-branding) and **Chehra** (soldier's descriptive roll) system.
keyPoints: Jalaluddin Khalji founded the dynasty in 1290; Alauddin Khalji seized power in 1296 (the 'Khalji revolution').
Alauddin's North Indian conquests: Gujarat, Ranthambore (1301), Chittor (1303), Malwa (1305); repelled the Mongols.
Malik Kafur's Deccan raids hit Devagiri (Yadava), Warangal (Kakatiya), Dwarasamudra (Hoysala) and Madurai (Pandya).
Market control: fixed low prices, markets (mandi, Sarai Adl), Shahna-i-Mandi supervisor and Diwan-i-Riyasat merchant registry.
Alauddin was first to keep a cash-paid standing army with the Dagh (branding) and Chehra (soldier roll) system.
items.mnemonic: Alauddin's army checks = 'Dagh brands the horse, Chehra describes the man.'

items.title: Tughlaq Dynasty — Experiments, Welfare & Timur
items.body:
## Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320–1325)

- Founder (defeated Khusrau Khan); built **Tughlaqabad Fort**; strengthened postal, judicial, irrigation and agricultural administration; harsh against the Mongols.

## Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq (1325–1351) — the 'failed experiments'

- **Capital transfer** from Delhi to **Daulatabad (Devagiri)**, later reversed; **token currency** of copper coins, soon withdrawn; **Doab tax rise** (peasant flight, famine); costly **Khurasan** and **Qarachil** (Himalayan) schemes. Sound ideas, poor implementation; **Ibn Battuta** served as a qazi in his reign.

## Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) — welfare king

- Dug irrigation **canals**; founded **Firozabad, Hissar, Jaunpur, Fatehabad**; built welfare bodies — **Dar-ul-Shafa** (hospital), **Diwan-i-Khairat** (marriage bureau), employment bureau; taxes = **Kharaj, Khams, Jizya, Zakat**; levied **jizya on Brahmins**; wrote **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi**; brought two **Ashokan pillars** to Delhi. But granting nobles autonomy weakened the centre.

## Decline

- After Firoz, weak successors; **Timur** of Samarqand sacked **Delhi in 1398**; the dynasty ended in **1414**.
keyPoints: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the dynasty in 1320 and built Tughlaqabad Fort.
Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's experiments: Daulatabad capital transfer, copper token currency, Doab tax rise, Khurasan/Qarachil schemes — all failed.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq built canals, towns and welfare institutions and imposed jizya on Brahmins.
Firoz Shah wrote Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi and brought two Ashokan pillars to Delhi.
Timur sacked Delhi in 1398; the Tughlaq dynasty ended in 1414, replaced by the Sayyids.

items.title: Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties — the Final Phase
items.body:
## Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451)

- Founded by **Khizr Khan** (Timur's former governor of Multan), who took the humble title **Rayat-i-Ala** and ruled in Timur's name; the rulers claimed descent from the **Prophet Muhammad** for legitimacy. **Mubarak Shah** dropped the nominal allegiance to Timur. The last ruler **Alam Shah** was displaced by **Bahlol Lodi** in 1451.

## Lodi dynasty (1451–1526) — first Afghan dynasty

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Bahlol Lodi | 1451–1489 | Founder; Pashtun (Afghan); consolidated Delhi |
| Sikandar Lodi | 1489–1517 | Founded **Agra** (1504); centralised administration |
| Ibrahim Lodi | 1517–1526 | Last Sultan; defeated & killed by **Babur at Panipat (1526)** |

- The Lodis were the **first Afghan (Pashtun)** dynasty; their tombs survive in the **Lodi Gardens**, Delhi.
keyPoints: Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414, used the title Rayat-i-Ala and ruled in Timur's name.
Sayyid rulers claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad; Mubarak Shah asserted independence from Timur.
Bahlol Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451 — the first Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty of Delhi.
Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra (1504) and centralised the administration.
Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan, was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

items.title: Administration, Iqta, Architecture & Sources
items.body:
## The iqta system & central administration

- The **iqta** was a **revenue assignment** (not hereditary land) given to nobles (**iqtadars/muqtis**) in return for maintaining troops — it linked the provinces to the centre and broke old feudal traditions.
- The Sultan headed a centralised state; key departments included the **Diwan-i-Wizarat** (finance), **Diwan-i-Arz** (military) and **Diwan-i-Insha** (correspondence).

## Indo-Islamic architecture

- Introduced the **true arch and dome**, minarets and use of mortar. Landmarks: **Qutub Minar** (begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish), **Alai Darwaza** (Alauddin, 1311 — first true dome/arch), **Tughlaqabad Fort** and **Firoz Shah Kotla**, and the **Lodi Gardens** tombs (octagonal tomb type).

## Literary sources

| Work | Author |
|---|---|
| Tabaqat-i-Nasiri | Minhaj-us-Siraj |
| Taj-ul-Maasir | Hasan Nizami |
| Khazain-ul-Futuh | Amir Khusrau |
| Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi | Ziauddin Barani |
| Rihla (Travels) | Ibn Battuta |
keyPoints: The iqta was a non-hereditary revenue assignment to nobles (muqtis) who maintained troops — the backbone of Sultanate administration.
Indo-Islamic architecture introduced the true arch and dome; the Alai Darwaza (1311) was the first true dome/arch in India.
Qutub Minar was begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish; Lodi Gardens preserve octagonal Sultanate tombs.
Amir Khusrau ('Parrot of India') wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh; Ziauddin Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi.
Ibn Battuta's Rihla describes India under Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq; Minhaj-us-Siraj wrote Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.
